scribe_response.text: Tell me about a journey you have never forgotten. One journey I have never forgotten um is the overnight train to Madras, when I was seventeen. I had been called to an interview for a seat at the engineering college there. My father bought me a second class ticket, and my mother packed lemon rice in a banana leaf. It was the first time I had travelled so far alone, and I felt very grown up. The carriage was crowded, with families on every um bench and baskets stacked in the um aisle. A ceiling fan turned lazily, and the wooden seats were polished by many years of travellers. The ticket collector punched my ticket with a small steel tool and wished me luck. Because the night was warm, I sat near the open door to catch the breeze. I had taken off my shoes and tucked them beside me, which was a terrible mistake. At some dark station the train lurched, my elbow knocked them, and my only pair of shoes fell out of the carriage door. I watched them tumble onto the track, and I could do nothing but stare. A kind old man nearby told me that the shoes had gone to a better place. I did not laugh, and I spent the night wondering what I would wear. What happened next? Rain began after midnight, and, and the smell of wet earth came through the door. The wheels beat a steady rhythm that I tried to count against my pulse. By morning the um sky was pink over the roofs of the city. At dawn in Madras a porter lent me a pair of rubber sandals that were two sizes too large. I flapped to the interview like a duck, and the, and the panel looked um at my feet with open amusement. I did not get the seat, but I did earn a few smiles. Apart from the shoes, the journey was a long lesson in how the country looked. The train ran through paddy fields shining with water, and later through dry red country dotted with palmyra trees. At every halt vendors rushed along the platform with tea, boiled eggs, and sweet crisp murukku. I leaned out of the window and listened to their cries, which rose and fell like a kind of music. At Palakkad the engine was changed, and I watched men uncouple it with enormous iron hooks. That was my first look at heavy machinery doing something with great calm precision. I memorised how the coupling worked, and I drew it in my notebook between two lines of arithmetic. Can you tell me more about that? A girl of about ten sat opposite me, and she shared her um tamarind sweets without saying a word. Her mother told me that they were travelling to see a grandfather who was very ill. I said a small prayer for him, and the girl solemnly nodded. When she got down at a small station, she waved with both hands until I could no longer see her. I still wonder what happened to that family and that grandfather. After the interview I walked to the beach and sat on the sand in my enormous sandals. It was my first view of a true ocean, and it was larger than any water I could imagine. The waves arrived in long grey lines and uh fell over themselves with a sound like distant trains. I felt tiny and, strangely, quite happy. The return journey was calmer, and a conductor found me a pair of canvas shoes at a station stall. When I came home, my sisters laughed for a week about the sandals. My father said that a man learns more from a lost shoe than from a found coin. I never took my shoes off near an open door again. In a sense that journey began my travelling life, though I did not know it then.
